Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

none pronoun

not one, not any

also none of them, none of us, none at all, none that I know of

classical

Hor. Ep. 1.1.75: nūlla retrōrsum
Cic. Off. 3.59: nūllae, quod sciam

nūllus, nūlla, nūllum

adjective used as a pronoun, in the gender of the noun understood; gen. nūllīus, dat. nūllī · Declension on Wiktionary

none, not one

Latin keeps the gender of what is meant: of footprints (vestīgia), nūlla; of holidays (fēriae), nūllae. Of two, “neither” is neuter (see neither); of a quantity, “none (of it)” is nihil (see nothing). A bare answer “none” is often the verb repeated with nōn.

Other words

  • nēmō, nēminis m. and f. — none (of persons): none of us, none of them

    pronoun; in classical Latin gen. nūllīus, abl. nūllō · also used · classical · Sen. Ep. 58.22: nēmō nostrum est īdem māne quī fuit prīdiē; Verg. A. 5.305: nēmō ex hōc numerō · Declension on Wiktionary

    For persons, with a genitive or ex for the group: nēmō nostrum, none of us; nēmō ex hōc numerō, none of this number. Lewis & Short: classical Latin supplies the genitive and ablative from nūllīus, nūllō.

Examples

  • quia mē vestīgia terrent, omnia tē adversum spectantia, nūlla retrōrsum

    because the footprints frighten me: all of them pointing towards you, none coming backHor. Ep. 1.1.74–75

  • ‘nūllae, quod sciam,’ ille, ‘sed hīc piscārī nūllī solent’

    (Was it some fishermen’s holiday?) ‘None that I know of,’ said he, ‘but nobody fishes here’Cic. Off. 3.59

  • utrumque enim vitium est, et omnibus crēdere et nūllī

    for both are faults, to trust everyone and to trust noneSen. Ep. 3.4

  • Quī omnēs īnsidiās timet, in nūllās incidit.

    Whoever fears every trap falls into none.Publil. Sent. Q 66

  • nēmō nostrum est īdem māne quī fuit prīdiē

    none of us is the same in the morning as he was the day beforeSen. Ep. 58.22

See also no, nothing, everyone, neither, one of.
